seoTitle: Open Multiple TradingView Charts Free with Vivaldi
metaDescription: See how to view multiple TradingView charts in one window for free using Vivaldi browser's split-screen tabs instead of a paid plan upgrade.
intro: TradingView's own multi-chart layouts are locked behind a paid plan, but you don't need one to watch several markets at once. The Vivaldi browser has tab tiling built in for free, and pointing it at a handful of TradingView tabs gets you the same side-by-side effect without upgrading anything. This guide covers getting Vivaldi installed, loading separate TradingView charts into its tabs, and tiling them into a single four-pane window you can actually trade from.

steps.heading: Download Vivaldi
steps.body: Head to vivaldi.com and grab the installer for your platform — the download page detects your OS automatically and offers a single button, with builds available for Windows, Mac, Linux, and Android. Vivaldi is a full Chromium-based browser, so anything that works in Chrome (extensions, bookmarks, autofill) carries over; the split-screen tiling used in this workflow is the feature that sets it apart and the reason to install it just for this.

image.caption: Vivaldi's download page, offering a single build for the detected operating system.

steps.heading: Load TradingView and sign in
steps.body: Open Vivaldi and navigate to TradingView like you would in any browser. Vivaldi's interface adds a slim icon rail down the left edge for its own panels — bookmarks, notes, mail, and so on — but the chart itself behaves identically to TradingView in Chrome or Firefox: same toolbar, same watch list on the right, same symbol search. Sign in and pull up the first chart you want in your layout before worrying about tiling anything.

image.caption: A single TradingView chart open in Vivaldi. The browser's own panel icons run down the far left edge.

steps.heading: Open additional charts in new tabs
steps.body: For each market you want to watch, open a new tab and load TradingView again, then search for the next symbol — a stock index, a crypto pair, a bond yield, whatever you're tracking in parallel. Each tab is a fully independent TradingView session, so different tabs can run different timeframes, indicators, and drawing tools without interfering with each other.

steps.heading: Tile the tabs into a split-screen layout
steps.body: With your tabs open, use Vivaldi's tab tiling to arrange them into a grid within one window instead of switching between tabs one at a time. The result is a single view split into quadrants, each running its own live TradingView chart — in the example here, the Dow Jones, Bitcoin, the US Composite Index, and the 10-year Treasury yield all update side by side in real time, each with its own toolbar and watch list still fully usable.

image.caption: Four TradingView tabs tiled into one Vivaldi window, each pane an independent, live-updating chart.

steps.heading: Fine-tune each pane for real-time tracking
steps.body: Once tiled, click into each pane individually to set its timeframe, add the indicators you use for that market, and confirm the price feed is live rather than paused. Because each pane is a separate tab under the hood, changes in one — switching from a 15-minute to an hourly candle, say — have no effect on the others, which is what makes this setup useful for comparing correlated markets at different resolutions.

steps.heading: Save the layout for next time
steps.body: Vivaldi can save a tiled group of tabs so you're not rebuilding the same four-chart arrangement from scratch every session — check your window or tab-stack options for a save or bookmark-as-session action. Reopening a saved layout brings back the same tab arrangement, though each TradingView chart will reload fresh, so any unsaved drawings or indicator tweaks from the previous session won't carry over automatically.

faq.question: Is this multi-chart method really free?
faq.answer: Yes, it relies on Vivaldi's free split-screen tab feature rather than any paid TradingView upgrade.

faq.question: Does this work for crypto, forex, and stocks at the same time?
faq.answer: Yes, since each tab loads TradingView independently, you can mix asset types across your split-screen layout.

faq.question: Will this slow down my computer with several charts open?
faq.answer: Running multiple live charts can use more system resources, so performance depends on your computer's specs and how many charts you keep open.

faq.question: Can I use this method on Chrome or another browser?
faq.answer: The split-screen tiling shown here is a Vivaldi-specific feature, so other browsers without similar tab-splitting tools won't replicate it the same way.
